extracted.intended_audience: members of Congress, legislative staff, USPTO officials, patent practitioners, biotech and diagnostics stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Legislative and managerial guidance on patent-policy provisions in the America Invents Act, including supplemental examination, a genetic-test study mandate, the Weldon prohibition on patenting human organisms, business-method transitional review, and USPTO fee access. Useful for interpreting how these provisions should be applied and implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and scope of Supplemental Examination
rubrics_metrics.description: This new 'Supplemental Examination' procedure encourages the voluntary and proactive disclosure of information that may be relevant to patent prosecution for the Office to consider, reconsider, or correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary disclosure by patentees serves to strengthen valid patents, while narrowing or eliminating patents or claims that should not have been issued. Both outcomes promote investment in innovation by removing uncertainty about the scope, validity or enforceability of patents, and thus the use of this new proceeding by patent owners is to be encouraged. The Director should implement this new authority in a way that maximizes this potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to Attorney General for potential fraud during Supplemental Examination or Reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: If, during supplemental examination or reexamination ordered under this section, a court or administrative agency advises the PTO that it has made a determination that a fraud on the Office may have been committed in connection with the patent that is the subject of the supplemental examination, the Director shall refer the matter to the Attorney General.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subparagraph © is not intended to impose any obligation on the PTO beyond those it already undertakes, or require it to investigate or prosecute any such potential fraud. It is neither an investigative nor an adjudicative provision and is not intended to expand the authority or obligation of the PTO to investigate or adjudicate allegations of fraud lodged by private parties. Any referral is not meant to relieve the Director from his obligation to conclude the supplemental examination or reexamination proceeding ordered under this section. The decision to make referrals under subsection © is not meant to be delegated to examiners or other agents of the PTO, but rather is a determination that should only be made by the Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic Test Study — assess availability and medical impact of confirmatory testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 27 requires the Director of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to conduct a study on the availability of confirmatory genetic diagnostic testing services in the domestic market, and whether changes to existing patent law are necessary to promote such availability more effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph (1) requires an assessment of whether the existing level of availability of confirmatory genetic diagnostic testing has an impact on the ability of medical professionals to provide the appropriate standard of medical care to recipients of genetic diagnostic testing, and includes an assessment of the role that patents play in innovation, quality of services, and investment in the genetic diagnostic marketplace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic Test Study — measure enforcement and comparative availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The study should include empirical information about the extent to which patents have actually been enforced or asserted against the unauthorized practice of confirmatory genetic diagnostic tests, and a comparison of the availability of and demand for confirmatory testing in situations where genetic tests are not patented or are non-exclusively licensed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include data on enforcement actions and compare markets with patented/exclusively-licensed tests versus non-patented or non-exclusively-licensed tests to evaluate effects on availability and demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic Test Study — assess effects on patent holders and providers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director must assess the effects of independent, unauthorized confirmatory genetic testing on patent holders or exclusively licensed test providers and consider effects on authorized providers of non-exclusively licensed genetic diagnostic tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee urges inclusion of possible effects on authorized non-exclusive providers, since such providers may already provide confirmatory testing services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic Test Study — evaluate impact on practice of medicine and frequency of confirmatory testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of the impact of patents and exclusive licensing of genetic diagnostic tests on the practice of medicine, including the ability of medical professionals to interpret test results, and the ability of licensed or unlicensed test providers to provide confirmatory genetic diagnostic tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should include information on the frequency at which confirmatory genetic diagnostic testing is currently performed by medical professionals in instances where absence of patent protection or non-exclusive licensing permits multiple independent test providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic Test Study — assess role of cost and insurance coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: An assessment of the role that cost and insurance coverage have on access to and provision of confirmatory genetic diagnostic tests today, whether patented or not or exclusively licensed or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should include an assessment of whether private and public payors cover such costs and are likely to cover the costs of any expansion of confirmatory testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weldon Amendment prohibition on patents 'directed to or encompassing a human organism'
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the funds appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be used to issue patents on claims directed to or encompassing a human organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prohibition limits the use of appropriated funds by the PTO to issue certain types of claims (specifically claims that encompass a human individual). It operates on patents that may issue on applications filed on or after the date of the legislation, does not create a cause of action, and does not alter rights associated with patents duly granted by the PTO. Because it addresses only appropriated funds, alternate funding (e.g., user fees) could affect its practical coverage unless codified into patent law.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO policy and MPEP guidance rejecting claims that encompass humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Longstanding USPTO practice: 'A claim directed to or including within its scope a human being will not be considered patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 101.' (Quigg memo / MPEP §2105).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Quigg memo and MPEP suggest including the limitation 'non-human' in claims that otherwise could be construed to encompass a human being to avoid a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection. If the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention as a whole encompasses a human being, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made indicating that the claimed invention is directed to nonstatutory subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of what Weldon does not affect (exceptions/clarifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Weldon Amendment does not limit patent eligibility for many biotechnology inventions and does not prevent patents on human cells, genes, or other tissues obtained from human embryos or human bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, nothing in this section should be construed to limit the PTO's ability to issue a patent containing claims directed to: (1) chemical compounds or compositions (including nucleic acids, polypeptides, proteins, antibodies and hormones); (2) cells, tissue, organs or other bodily components produced through human intervention (including stem cells, stem cell derived tissues, stem cell lines, and viable synthetic organs); (3) methods for creating, modifying, or treating human organisms (e.g., IVF, somatic cell nuclear transfer, medical or genetic therapies); or (4) a nonhuman organism incorporating one or more genes taken from a human organism (e.g., transgenic animals). Rep. Weldon and others clarified the amendment does not affect patents for non-human organisms even with some human genes, nor patents for human cells, tissues, organs, methods, drugs, or devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business-Method Transitional Review — purpose and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The proceeding would create a cheap and speedy alternative to litigation—allowing parties to resolve these disputes rather than spend millions of dollars that litigation now costs; preventing nuisance or extortion litigation settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision allows business-method patents to be reviewed by PTO experts under the correct (Bilski) standard. Resolving validity through this administrative proceeding costs much less than civil litigation and provides a fast, precise vehicle to review low quality business method patents that are often abstract and overly broad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility threshold for Business-Method Transitional Review
rubrics_metrics.description: To use this proceeding, a challenger must make an up-front showing to the PTO of evidence that the business-method patent is more likely than not invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a high standard intended to limit review to the worst patents. The challenger must present best evidence and arguments at the outset; only patents that are likely invalid under Bilski will be eligible for review. Very few patents that undergo this review are likely to be valid patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional authority and precedent for administrative review of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has the authority to create administrative proceedings to review the validity of existing patents; prior examples (e.g., ex parte reexam in 1980) and Federal Circuit precedent (Patlex Corp. v. Mossinghoff) reject 'taking' arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section only creates a new mechanism for reviewing validity and does not alter substantive law governing validity. Under settled precedent, applying administrative review to existing patents is constitutional and not a taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO fee access and fee-diversion concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing USPTO access to all fees collected means providing access at all points during that year, including in case of a continuing resolution. USPTO is 100% funded by fees paid by inventors and trademark filers who are entitled to receive the services they are paying for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fee diversion (Congressional siphoning of USPTO-collected fees) has led to backlog and delay; the Manager's Amendment language reflects intent to end fee diversion and to appropriate to the USPTO any fees collected in excess of appropriation. Access also means timely action on reprogramming requests and guarantees for future appropriations language to ensure USPTO access to its fee collections.
